prompt: Which is the strongest acid (lowest pKa)?
explanation: Carboxylic acids are far more acidic than alcohols/water/amines due to resonance stabilization of the carboxylate conjugate base.

prompt: Why is a carboxylic acid more acidic than an alcohol with the same R group?
choices: The carboxylate anion delocalizes negative charge over two oxygens by resonance
explanation: Resonance delocalization in the carboxylate (RCOO-) stabilizes the conjugate base far more than a single localized alkoxide (RO-).

prompt: Phenol (pKa ~10) is more acidic than cyclohexanol (pKa ~16, a plain alcohol) because:
choices: Phenol's conjugate base (phenoxide) is resonance-stabilized by the aromatic ring
The OH bond is longer in phenol
explanation: The phenoxide negative charge delocalizes into the ring, stabilizing it relative to a simple alkoxide.

prompt: Rank acidity (most to least acidic): terminal alkyne C-H (pKa ~25), alkane C-H (pKa ~50), water (pKa ~15.7).
explanation: Water is far more acidic than either C-H bond; among the C-H bonds, sp-hybridized alkyne C-H (more s-character, electrons held closer) is more acidic than sp3 alkane C-H.

prompt: Protonated amine (ammonium, RNH3+, pKa ~10-11) vs neutral amine — which is the acid in this conjugate pair?
choices: RNH3+ is the acid, RNH2 is the conjugate base
RNH2 is the acid, RNH3+ is the conjugate base
Neither is an acid or base
explanation: RNH3+ can donate a proton to become RNH2 — the protonated (charged) form is always the acid in the pair.

prompt: Which best explains why HCl (pKa ~ -7) is a much stronger acid than HF (pKa ~3.2)?
choices: Cl is more electronegative than F
The H-Cl bond is weaker and easier to break than H-F, and Cl- is a larger, more stable anion
HF is not a real acid
explanation: Down a group, bond strength drops faster than electronegativity effects matter; the larger, more polarizable Cl- anion is more stable, making HCl the far stronger acid.

prompt: An alpha-hydrogen next to a carbonyl (e.g. in acetone, pKa ~20) is more acidic than a typical alkane C-H (pKa ~50) because:
choices: The resulting enolate anion is resonance-stabilized by the adjacent carbonyl
explanation: Deprotonation gives an enolate whose negative charge delocalizes onto the electronegative carbonyl oxygen — a very common orgo acidity comparison.

prompt: Adding electron-withdrawing groups (like additional Cl atoms) near an acidic proton generally makes that proton:
explanation: Electron-withdrawing groups stabilize the resulting negative charge inductively, increasing acidity — e.g. trichloroacetic acid is far more acidic than acetic acid.

prompt: For an acid-base reaction to be favorable (favor products) at equilibrium, you generally want:
choices: The acid on the reactant side to have a HIGHER pKa than the acid formed on the product side
The acid on the reactant side to have a LOWER pKa than the acid formed on the product side
pKa values don't matter for equilibrium position
Both acids must have identical pKa
explanation: The reaction proceeds toward the weaker acid (higher pKa); if the starting acid is stronger (lower pKa) than what's formed, the forward reaction is favored.

choices: Conjugate base of a strong acid (e.g. Cl-)
Conjugate base of a weak acid (e.g. the amide ion, NH2-, conjugate base of NH3 with pKa ~38)
explanation: The weaker the acid, the stronger its conjugate base — NH2- (from very weak acid NH3) is an extremely strong base.
